Testing times: On India’s two-Test series against New Zealand
 India needs to be at its best in Tests against New Zealand
 Updated - November 19, 2026 12:28 pm IST 
 READ LATER 
 SEE ALL 
 Remove 
 New Zealand at home remains an indomitable cricketing opposition. Even the great West Indian squad led by Clive Lloyd suffered a 0-1 Test series defeat in 1980. Pitches that look lush as English meadows, the wind that is often bone-chilling cold, and fast bowlers relishing their prospects, make any tour of New Zealand a difficult outing. So far, the visiting Indians have done well, having won the T20I and ODI series, but the real contest starts with the first Test at Wellington’s Basin Reserve from Thursday. The Shubman Gill-led men’s last overseas tour of Sri Lanka ended with a middling 1-0 victory in the two Tests, but more needs to be done against New Zealand in the latest two-Test series. Placed fourth in the ICC World Test Championship (WTC) table, and with hopes of securing a final berth seemingly fragile, India is in a win-all-games situation first up against New Zealand and later when Australia arrives next year. Against current WTC topper New Zealand, the Indian batters have to stay anchored. This is a line-up that no longer has Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, Cheteshwar Pujara and Ajinkya Rahane. Gill and company get another opportunity to reiterate their credentials.
 For some rugged inspiration they need not look beyond coach Gautam Gambhir in their dressing room. The doughty former India opener batted for 643 minutes while scoring a match-saving 137 in the Napier Test during the 2009 tour. The southpaw will be hoping that the current batting unit, which is high on flair, will remain sober and effectively counter the host. K.L. Rahul, Yashasvi Jaiswal, Devdutt Padikkal and Gill have the onerous task of negating the New Zealand seamers in their backyard. Rishabh Pant and Dhruv Jurel add depth, and if the former can successfully unleash his maverick batting approach, India can upset the host’s best-laid plans. New Zealand will miss the retired Kane Williamson but its batters would be comfortable on familiar surfaces. For India, much would hinge on how Jasprit Bumrah bowls. If the spearhead clicks, then it becomes easier for much of his support-cast that includes the persevering Mohammed Siraj, who was a touch rusty in Sri Lanka. From the squads of the past to the present unit, Ravindra Jadeja remains the link. Whether he will get a role to play or whether the management prefers an all-pace attack, remains a matter of conjecture. The home team led by Tom Latham will depend on Matt Henry, Kyle Jameson and other pacers, to choke the Indian batters. A hard task awaits India, first at Wellington and then at Christchurch.
